chunks.adarle20:how-he-built-it:
A Darle 20 — How he built it
He built the platform as sole developer using AI-native workflows (AI coding tools), owning the architecture, code review and release. The stack: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase (PostgreSQL), Stripe Connect, Vercel, PostHog and Resend.
chunks.adarle20:overview:
A Darle 20 — A Darle 20
A Darle 20 ("Let's Go 20") is a marketplace for tabletop game sessions, live at adarle20.com and based in Puebla, Mexico. Hosts list sessions and players reserve them. Sidhant's role: co-founder and CTO, part-time and remote, and the sole developer. He started in August 2025 and it launched in March 2026.
chunks.adarle20:the-convention-event:
A Darle 20 — The convention event
He ran the technology behind a flagship 251-player event at a 19,000-attendee convention, rated 4.96/5 by attendees.
chunks.adarle20:what-the-data-showed:
A Darle 20 — What the data showed
He instrumented the funnel: conversion, refunds and host activation. The data showed paid acquisition wasn't worth it, so growth runs on in-person marketing and word of mouth.
chunks.adarle20:where-it-stands:
A Darle 20 — Where it stands
It has reached 2,100+ users, 110+ hosts and 3,600+ session reservations from 1,000+ players. The exact counts from the production database on October 25, 2026: 2,189 users, 111 hosts who have listed a session, and 3,641 confirmed reservations from 1,057 players. About 84% of sessions are free, so these are session reservations rather than paid sales.
chunks.bio:overview:
About — About Sidhant
Sidhant Mathur is a sales operations specialist at Nokia, where he has worked since October 2021, and the co-founder and CTO of A Darle 20, part-time. He lives in Toronto, ON.
He's an ops person whose edge is building. He builds and runs the tools a 7-region sales organization reports on, and he inherits and keeps alive the ones other people built.
chunks.dell:overview:
Dell — Propensity model at Dell
A cross-sell propensity model, built as an intern. Sidhant's role: marketing intern at Dell Technologies in Round Rock, TX, May 2018 – Aug 2018.
He built a propensity model in Azure ML that found about 20,000 cross-sell accounts. At the segment's average deal size, those accounts are worth about $129M. That figure is a sizing (accounts times average deal size), not pipeline. He then trained the sales and marketing teams to use the model's output for lead prioritization.
chunks.nokia:overview:
Nokia — Reporting and tooling at Nokia
Sidhant has been at Nokia since October 2021: workforce management specialist in Ottawa from Oct 2021 to Jun 2024, then sales operations specialist, based in Toronto and remote, from Jun 2024 to the present. He builds and runs the tools a 7-region sales organization reports on, and he inherits and keeps alive the ones other people built. The work is internal to Nokia, so there are no screenshots.
chunks.nokia:quarter-end-close:
Nokia — Quarter-end close
He launched the self-serve Power App behind quarter-end executive reporting, used by 80+ stakeholders across 7 regions. It replaced a full-day manual consolidation by one finance analyst that was error-prone under close deadlines. Close reporting no longer waits on one person.
chunks.nokia:reporting:
Nokia — Reporting
He delivered Salesforce CRM Analytics dashboards for exec reviews, with 150+ monthly users, then moved reporting to Power BI. He also built Power BI reports for 5 teams outside the sales organization and maintains the automation that keeps them refreshed. His Salesforce work is reports and dashboards in CRM Analytics, not administration: no flows, validation rules or data loads.
chunks.nokia:scale:
Nokia — Scale
The sales organization spans 7 regions and has $10B+ in pipeline. That is the organization's scale, not a pipeline he carries.
chunks.nokia:the-ai-agent-in-testing:
Nokia — The AI agent, in testing
He is building an AI agent on Power BI, Glean and Teams that flags pipeline gaps against prior years, conflicting fields and past-due dates. Power BI does the bulk analysis and segmentation; Glean is the reasoning layer. It is in testing, not live, and has no results yet.
chunks.nokia:the-weekly-operating-review-tool:
Nokia — The weekly operating review tool
Regional sales ops teams use it to compile the Chief Customer Officer's weekly report. It merges CRM data with standardized self-serve updates, which replaced ad hoc email, meetings and slides. He shipped it within two weeks of the process launching, and regions also run their own reviews on it. He builds and maintains the tool. He doesn't attend or own the meeting, and the record doesn't say what the Chief Customer Officer takes from the report.
chunks.nokia:what-he-inherited:
Nokia — What he inherited
He inherited the Power App and automations that North America runs its reviews on from a developer who moved teams, and he has extended them. North America runs its monthly reviews, incentive performance reviews and weekly operating review on it. It has about 30 core users: North America sales ops and some sales leaders.
He also runs the queries and automations behind monthly and quarterly sales incentive calculations for 900+ staff: about 200 account managers and about 700 pre-sales and customer success staff. North America is monthly; the other regions are quarterly. He inherited the process, cut steps and manual checks from the automation, and made it faster. He has no authority over incentive design.
chunks.nokia:workforce-management:
Nokia — Workforce management
As a workforce management specialist, Oct 2021 – Jun 2024, he ran the monthly headcount forecast process, plus planning and requisitions, for a 3,000–4,000-person organization. Headcount was about 70% of the organization's budget. His manager owned the process; he did nearly all the work.
He automated the forecast's input checks with VBA, saving about 5 hours a week of manual review: his predecessor spent about an hour a day checking team inputs by hand. He inherited and ran the SharePoint home site for the same 3,000–4,000 people and was the go-to person for teams setting up their own sites.
He led a lab and facility utilization analysis that identified $1.2M in real-estate cost savings. The savings were identified, not necessarily realized.
